paras: The killing of Ed Nelms was the fatal shooting of Ed Nelms, a Black man who had escaped from a Mississippi jail while under sentence of death, by Memphis Chief of Police W. C. Davis on the Arkansas bank of the Mississippi River opposite Memphis early on December 29, 1881. A coroner's jury at Memphis found the same day that Davis was "thoroughly justifiable." The Memphis dailies praised the chief at length, and a brief dispatch carried the story nationwide.

Nelms had twice been convicted of the May 9, 1880, ambush killing of Rufus Armistead, a plantation manager south of Memphis, and sentenced to hang, but the Mississippi Supreme Court stayed the execution. At his capture in 1880 he had been tracked "by dogs and men" to the canebrakes of Tunica County, and the Public Ledger said several Black men who sheltered him were later murdered by masked men who were never punished. A Memphis dispatch of December 23, 1881, reported that all the prisoners in the jail at Hernando, Mississippi, had escaped, Nelms among them; the Ledger instead said four others fled with him from "the Senatobia prison."

On the night of December 28 Davis learned that Nelms's uncle, Riley, had arranged for a skiff to carry Nelms across the river at midnight. Davis, Captain Pat Hackett and others crossed to the Arkansas side and waited in a laborer's cabin; when no boat came, all but Davis, Hackett and a laborer, A. Bodkins, went home.

At about half past one a skiff with four men approached, and Davis, posing as a railroad worker, had Bodkins call them to land near the officers. Davis and Hackett covered Riley, who carried a shotgun and surrendered. In the officers' account as both Memphis papers printed it, Nelms crouched and backed away reaching for a pistol, ignored two commands to surrender, and was shot in the head when Davis, saying he aimed to cripple him, fired. A navy revolver was reported found beneath the body, and the other men were taken to the city prison.

Armistead's relatives, a Mississippi jail officer and one of the Black jurors from Nelms's trial identified the body. At 11 o'clock Justice P. J. Quigley held an inquest at Memphis, hearing Davis, Hackett, Bodkins, Isaac Riley, John Armistead and DeSoto County jailer W. H. Rollins. Two physicians gave the opinion that Nelms had been standing with his breast toward the chief and his head turned slightly left. The jury found that Davis fired in Crittenden County, Arkansas, at a fugitive convicted of murder, and was "thoroughly justifiable."

Davis told the Crittenden County sheriff he would answer for the shooting there, but no report of an Arkansas proceeding appears in the coverage. In January 1882 the Memphis council rejected a $15 claim for the wagon that carried the remains, and the Appeal objected that the petition noted Nelms and another man had been "killed by police officers."

The Memphis papers treated the killing as police courage. The Public Ledger headlined it "IN HIS COFFIN," calling Nelms "A Desperate Darky" who "Meets his Just Reward." The Appeal called Davis a chief "who hardly knows what fear is," pictured Nelms crouching "like the wild beast he is," and said he "was no better than a dog."

Elsewhere the story ran as a short Memphis dispatch, printed on December 30 from Los Angeles and Cheyenne to Knoxville, Savannah, Virginia and New York, and in weeklies into January. It called Nelms "the negro murderer" under headlines such as "Shot by Police" and "Negro Desperado Killed."

The dispatch said Nelms tried to shoot but his gun "missed fire" and that his party was "well armed with shot guns and pistols," while the Ledger said Riley "apparently was the only one of them armed." The dispatch also placed Captains Hackett and "O'Haver" beside Davis instead of Bodkins, and counted six or sixteen escapees rather than the Ledger's four. The local stories are fuller and include the inquest, but every version of the shooting came from the officers' side, and no account of it by Riley or the boatmen was printed.

bases: Memphis Chief of Police W. C. Davis, with a police captain and a laborer, shot dead an escaped prisoner he was trying to recapture; no crowd took part (A3, A5, A22).
Two Memphis dailies and a separate wire dispatch agree that Chief Davis shot and killed Nelms as his party landed on the Arkansas shore, and the inquest verdict confirms it (A3, A5, A8, A9).

accounts.label: Memphis police account (local papers)
accounts.gist: Davis and Hackett covered Riley; Nelms, uncovered, crouched, backed away reaching for a pistol and ignored two commands to surrender; Davis fired meaning to hit his legs and struck his temple; a navy revolver was found clutched under the body.

accounts.label: Wire dispatch
accounts.gist: Commanded to halt, Nelms tried to shoot but his gun missed fire, and Davis then fired; the whole party was well armed with shotguns and pistols and his companions were jailed.

accounts.label: Coroner's jury
accounts.gist: Nelms died of a gunshot wound to the head fired by W. C. Davis in Crittenden County, Arkansas, while a fugitive convicted of first-degree murder; Davis was 'thoroughly justifiable'.

accounts.label: Inquest physicians
accounts.gist: Nelms must have been standing with his breast toward the Chief and his head turned a little to the left (the rest of the passage is cut off).

framing.detail: The Public Ledger headlined 'IN HIS COFFIN. A Desperate Darky Crossed the River of Death' and said Nelms 'Meets his Just Reward'.
The Memphis Appeal praised Davis as fearless, compared Nelms to a 'wild beast' and a panther, and said he 'was no better than a dog' whom none would regret.
Papers nationwide ran the Memphis dispatch calling Nelms 'the negro murderer' under heads like 'Shot by Police', 'An Escaping Murderer Killed' and 'Negro Desperado Killed'.
